findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Investment income on track with elevated rates supporting Q1 performance
findings.detail: The council's investment income performance is tracking to budget with elevated market rates during Q1 2026/27. By 30 June 2026, the council had secured £0.251m against its full-year budget of £1.1m. Officers confirm that approved investment limits were not breached and continue to monitor counterparty creditworthiness.
findings.matters: Shows council is capturing budgeted investment returns and maintaining investment discipline
findings.figures: 2026/27 investment income budget: £1.1m; secured to 30 June: £0.251m; funds available for investment: £25.9m
findings.quote: The Council's budget for in-house investment income in 2026/27 is £1.1m. On 30th June, the Council had secured a return of £0.251m.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Council relies on internal borrowing to fund capital; reserves will require future replenishment
findings.detail: The council has been in an internally borrowed cash position for several years, funding capital schemes from reserves rather than external borrowing. Officers plan to maintain this strategy while investment rates remain lower than borrowing rates, but balances will need replenishing subject to expenditure demands. Officers closely monitor reserves, balances and cashflows supporting this position.
findings.matters: Shows council's capital funding depends on finite reserve depletion; future spending will require either external borrowing or reserve rebuilding
findings.figures: External debt (excluding Finance Leases) £4m at 30 June 2026; funds available for investment £25.9m
findings.quote: For several years, the Council has been in an internally borrowed cash position, and balances will need to be replenished at some point in the future, subject to expenditure demands.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Council increases borrowing limits after correcting prior-year IFRS 16 treatment of finance lease
findings.detail: An error in implementing IFRS 16 on a finance lease in 2024/25 was identified during the audit and has been corrected with specialist advice. As a result, if the council were to borrow externally for all approved capital schemes, it would exceed existing prudential limits. The council therefore proposes to increase Operational Boundary from £20.7m to £22.224m and Authorised Limit from £23m to £25.3m.
findings.matters: Reveals accounting restatement, shows extent of council's committed capital spending, and increases approved debt capacity
findings.figures: Operational Boundary: £20,700,000 to £22,224,000; Authorised Limit: £23,000,000 to £25,300,000
findings.quote: Following the Audit of the Financial Accounts for 2024/25, Officers became aware of an error in the way in which IFRS16 was implemented on a finance lease in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: Regular public sector pay growth accelerated to 5.1% three-monthly year-on-year, up from 4.8%
findings.detail: While private sector pay growth has eased to 3.4% excluding bonuses, regular public sector pay growth accelerated from 4.8% to 5.1% three-monthly year-on-year. This means council payroll costs are growing significantly faster than CPI inflation of 2.8%, creating sustained budget pressure across local authorities.
findings.matters: Payroll typically represents 60-70% of council spending; pay growth outpacing inflation creates budget pressure
findings.figures: Public sector pay 5.1% vs private sector 3.4% (ex-bonus) vs CPI 2.8%
findings.quote: regular public sector pay growth accelerated from 4.8% 3myy to 5.1% 3myy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: Public sector net borrowing £23.3bn in May, £5.4bn above May 2025 and above OBR forecast
findings.detail: Government borrowing in May reached £23.3bn, £5.4bn higher than May 2025 and above the OBR's forecast of £17.7bn. Debt interest payments hit £4.1bn above May 2025 (the highest in any May on record) and £3.3bn above OBR prediction. Government borrowing forecast to rise from 4.2% of GDP in 2025/26 to 4.4% in 2026/27, reflecting fiscal pressure affecting market conditions for local authority borrowing.
findings.matters: Higher government borrowing affects gilt market conditions and availability of funding for local authorities
findings.figures: £23.3bn (vs £17.7bn forecast), £5.4bn above May 2025, borrowing forecast rising to 4.4% from 4.2% of GDP
findings.quote: Public sector net borrowing of £23.3bn in May was above the OBR's forecast of £17.7bn and £5.4bn above May's figure last year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: Employment fell 0.4% year-on-year with claimant count at largest monthly rise since July 2024
findings.detail: May employment rose only 2,000, barely offsetting a 53,000 fall in April, leaving employment 64,000 (0.2%) below pre-Iran war levels and 0.4% below a year ago. Job vacancies fell for the fourth consecutive month and the claimant count saw its largest monthly rise since July 2024.
findings.matters: Falling employment and rising claimant count increase demand for council welfare services and reduce the local tax base
findings.figures: Employment 64,000 (0.2%) below pre-war, 0.4% below year-ago, largest claimant rise since July 2024
findings.quote: that barely offset the big 53,000 drop in April and meant employment was still 64,000 (0.2%) lower than before the s tart of the Iran war and 0.4% lower than a year ago

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: Ofgem utility price cap rising 13.5% taking effect from 1 July, adding 0.6 percentage points to CPI
findings.detail: The 13.5% rise in the Ofgem utility price cap takes effect from 1 July 2026, adding 0.6 percentage points to CPI inflation. This represents a direct increase in council operating costs for energy, which will erode the resources available for service delivery.
findings.matters: Direct impact on council's energy costs reduces resources available for service delivery
findings.figures: 13.5% rise, adding 0.6 ppts to CPI from 1 July
findings.quote: The 13.5% rise in the Ofgem utility price cap, which will add 0.6 percentage points (ppts) to CPI inflation, doesn't take effect until 1 st July.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: 10-year gilt yields reached 5.18% in mid-May (highest since 2008) before falling back to 4.7%
findings.detail: Yields rose from 4.92% at end of March to 5.18% in mid-May, marking the highest level since 2008, driven by energy prices, inflation concerns and UK political risk premium. Following developments in the Iran conflict and fall in oil prices, yields fell back to 4.7% by June, supported by Bank of England holding rates and improved fiscal outlook.
findings.matters: Gilt yield movements directly affect the cost at which councils can borrow for capital projects and refinancing
findings.figures: 5.18% (peak May), 4.92% (end March), 4.7% (June), fluctuated between 5.18% and 4.69%
findings.quote: the 10-year Gilt shot up to 5.18% in mid-May, its highest level since 2008

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Economic Update
findings.headline: Economic growth turned negative in April with 0.1% m/m fall in real GDP, the first decline since August 2025
findings.detail: After strong growth of 0.6% q/q in Q4 2025/early 2026, the economy faltered in April. Services output contracted 0.2% m/m with consumer-facing services recording its biggest monthly fall since May 2025 as households cut back on non-energy spending. The services PMI fell to a 41-month low of 48.7 in June.
findings.matters: Declining economic growth affects local tax base and increases demand for council services including welfare support
findings.figures: 0.1% m/m fall in April, 0.6% q/q Jan-March, services output -0.2% m/m, services PMI 48.7
findings.quote: The first sign that the economy is starting to falter with a 0.1% m/m fall in real GDP in April

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Capital Programme Review 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants service provider undergoing review to address delivery capacity
findings.detail: Lightbulb service provider subject to streamlining review aimed at increasing DFG throughput; £846k of planned Q1 spend remained unspent, indicating delivery constraint or timing issue. Council expects review outcome to improve number of DFGs completed in remainder of year.
findings.matters: DFGs are statutory demand-led service for disabled residents; significant Q1 underspend combined with active service review signals council recognized delivery constraint and is implementing corrective action
findings.figures: £846,007 planned spend not yet utilised in Q1
findings.quote: Lightbulb has been subject to a service review to streamline ways of working which will increase the number of DFG's completed throughout the year.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Capital Programme Review 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Council investing £3.5m in properties to address temporary accommodation demand through capital programme
findings.detail: Council has paid deposits on 41 properties (6 at Little Glen, 35 at Countesthorpe) with further milestone payments planned during 2026/27. This represents a strategic shift from revenue-funded temporary placements to capital-backed ownership of permanent stock.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation cost is a significant and growing pressure on English councils; this capital investment approach signals a fundamental strategic change in service provision model with ongoing implications for debt servicing, operational costs, and balance-sheet structure
findings.figures: £3,468,609 budgeted for property investment programme; deposits paid on 41 properties with milestone payments planned throughout 2026/27; £607k identified for temporary accommodation pressure relief
findings.quote: Deposits for the purchase of 6 properties at Little Glen and 35 properties at Countesthorpe have been paid. Further milestone payments will be made during the year as the construction of the properties continue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Monitoring Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund delivering at 99% pace, spent £664k of £669k in Q1
findings.detail: UK Shared Prosperity Fund has spent £664k by end of Q1 with only £4.3k variance remaining, contrasting sharply with portfolio-wide underspend. This demonstrates the council's execution capability and ability to deploy capital rapidly when programmes are managed actively.
findings.matters: Counter-signals portfolio-wide underspend concerns; shows council has execution capacity and can deploy capital when required, mitigating (but not resolving) questions about delivery capability
findings.figures: UK Shared Prosperity Fund £668,718 approved, £664,378 spent (99.3% deployed)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Monitoring Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: Regeneration Property (largest capital project at £4.47m) shows 78% unspent at end of Q1
findings.detail: Regeneration Property is the single largest capital commitment, budgeted as an Invest to Save scheme. Only £996k (22%) has been spent by end of June, leaving £3.47m undeployed. This is the flagship scheme in the portfolio and its delivery trajectory will substantially affect overall programme performance.
findings.matters: Large capital projects indicate council delivery capability; slow progress on the largest scheme raises execution questions and affects credibility of capital plans
findings.figures: Regeneration Property £4,465,384 latest approved, £996,775 spent, £3,468,609 variance (78% unspent)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Monitoring Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: Capital programme 86% underspent in Q1, with multiple projects unstarted
findings.detail: £1.18m of £8.54m capital programme deployed by end of June. Fleet Vehicle Replacement (£671k), Provision for IT Infrastructure Improvements (£125k), Strategic Review for Land Rear of Enderby Leisure Centre (£221k) show zero expenditure. Regeneration Property, largest scheme at £4.47m, is 78% unspent at £3.47m variance.
findings.matters: Significant Q1 underspend raises questions about whether budgets will be fully deployed and on timeline, affecting cash flow and delivery risk assessment
findings.figures: £1,179,492 of £8,538,488 spent (86% variance); Fleet Vehicle Replacement £671,307 with £0 spent; Provision for IT Infrastructure Improvements £125,904 with £0 spent

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Capital Monitoring Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: Council approves £3.77m of prudential borrowing for 2026/27 capital programme
findings.detail: Prudential borrowing represents 44% of total capital financing for the year. This is new internal borrowing to fund capital schemes including regeneration, IT systems, and vehicle replacement. Increases the council's debt burden and future interest payment obligations.
findings.matters: Prudential borrowing increases council's indebtedness; lenders assess debt strategy and capacity when determining credit terms and risk
findings.figures: £3,772,143 approved prudential borrowing out of £8,538,488 total programme (44%)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Forecasting Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: HR & Payroll System project incomplete at planned June 2026 end date
findings.detail: The HR & Payroll System budgeted at £62,722 with a planned June 2026 completion shows only £16,163 spent by period end, leaving £46,559 underspent and indicating the project extended beyond its completion deadline. The project still shows as 'In progress' despite having reached its planned end date.
findings.matters: A missed system completion deadline, particularly for core HR and payroll functions, indicates project management issues and may affect operational stability if the delay continues
findings.figures: £62,722 budget; £16,163 forecast spend; £46,559 underspend
findings.quote: HR & Payroll System Jun-25 Jun-26 13 In progress 62,722 16,163 (46,559) -

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Forecasting Statement to 30th June 2026
findings.headline: Fleet Vehicle Replacement Programme £510,000 slippage (76% of £671,307 budget)
findings.detail: The Fleet Vehicle Replacement Programme started April 2026 with March 2028 planned completion shows £510,000 of its £671,307 budget pushed to future years, with only £161,307 forecast to be spent in the current financial year. Despite being three months into a 24-month project, over three-quarters of the budget is undeployed.
findings.matters: Significant slippage on a major capital asset replacement programme indicates procurement delays or delivery risks that affect fleet service continuity and may signal broader council capital programme management issues

findings.headline: Walk & Ride Blaby project completely slipped with £124,000 pushed to future years
findings.detail: The Walk & Ride Blaby project, which started June 2024 with a planned December 2027 completion, shows its entire £124,000 budget recorded as slippage with £0 forecast spending in 2026/27. After 24 months, the project has recorded no capital spend.
findings.matters: Complete slippage on a multi-year project indicates significant delivery delays and raises questions about the council's project delivery capability and whether this reflects procurement, resourcing, or supplier challenges

findings.quote: Walk & Ride Blaby Jun-24 Dec-27 43 In progress 124,000 - - 124,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix D – Treasury and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Lothbury Property Trust investment wound up; final distribution to UBS Triton completed April 2026.
findings.detail: The council's £1m investment in Lothbury Property Trust (made December 2019) has been transferred as capital distributions to UBS Triton Property Fund LP following the winding up of Lothbury. The final distribution was completed 30 April 2026. The investment value at 30 June 2026 is £744,968, and the council maintains an earmarked reserve of £228,982 for interest from the property fund.
findings.matters: Portfolio changes matter to lenders assessing councils' asset positions and investment strategy; the wind-up is recent (within months of this paper).
findings.figures: Original investment December 2019: £1m; value at 30 June 2026: £744,968; earmarked reserve: £228,982
findings.quote: The investment has been transferred as capital distributions to UBS (UBS Triton property fund LP) following the winding up of the Lothbury fund. The final distribution was made on 30th April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D – Treasury and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement for 2026/27 increased to £3.77m from approved budget of £2.63m.
findings.detail: The council's estimated borrowing need has risen by £1.15m (44%) due to the larger capital programme and associated financing gap. This reflects the council's assessment of cash needed to fund the revised capital plans.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing requirements signal expanding capital activity and indicate whether the council's debt position remains within prudential limits and headroom.
findings.figures: Borrowing Requirement: £2,627,099 (approved) to £3,772,143 (revised)
findings.quote: Borrowing Requirement 2,627,099 7,401 3,772,143

findings.paper_title: Appendix D – Treasury and Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Capital programme for 2026/27 revised to £8.5m, a 69% increase from approved budget of £5.1m.
findings.detail: The approved capital budget was £5.1m; the revised estimate is £8.5m. This includes £3.4m of expenditure and resources brought forward from 2025/26. The associated Capital Financing Requirement has increased from £23.4m (approved) to £24.2m (revised).
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' capital delivery capacity and ability to finance expanded programmes; material in-year increases signal either genuine new opportunities or risks in the baseline budget.
findings.figures: Total Capital Programme: £5,066,884 (approved) to £8,538,488 (revised); brought forward: £3,445,644; CFR: £23,429,609 to £24,175,389
findings.quote: The Revised Capital Programme includes expenditure and resources brought forward from 2025/26 totalling £3,445,644.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive - Treasury Management Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Property fund investment remains in loss with incomplete reserve coverage against further deterioration
findings.detail: The Council invested £1m in Lothbury Property Trust in December 2019. Following termination of that fund in 2024, the investment was transferred to UBS Triton. The UBS Triton value as at 31 March 2025 was £745,238.18, representing an unrealized loss of approximately £255k. The council has explicitly identified this as a risk: that the UBS Triton investment will not achieve full recovery of the loss. An earmarked reserve of £228,982.78 exists but does not cover the full initial investment.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of the council's exposure to unrealized investment losses and whether reserves are adequate to mitigate further declines that could impair the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Initial investment: £1m (Dec 2019); UBS Triton value (31 March 2025): £745,238.18; Unrealized loss: ~£255k; Earmarked reserve: £228,982.78
findings.quote: An earmarked reserve is in place to mitigate any potential fluctuations in the fund value, although it does not cover the full value of the initial investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Appendices 2026/27
findings.headline: General fund reserves forecast to decline 63% from £18.4m in 2025/26 to £6.7m by 2030/31 while council maintains under-borrowed position
findings.detail: Fund Balances & Reserves projected to fall from £18,381k (2025/26 revised) to £6,724k (2030/31), a decline of £11.7m over four years. This depletion occurs while the council maintains an under-borrowed position, choosing to fund capital investment through reserves and cash rather than borrowing. Strategy is described as prudent because the council expects medium and longer-term borrowing rates to fall from current elevated levels.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to this extent significantly reduces financial resilience and ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. Simultaneously, under-borrowing defers locking in current borrowing rates and creates exposure to rate risk if rates do not fall as forecast. A reserves base of £6.7m may be insufficient if the council faces unexpected challenges. Lenders assess financial stability; rapid reserve depletion indicates deteriorating financial position.
findings.figures: Fund Balances & Reserves £18,381k (2025/26) declining to £6,724k (2030/31); reduction of £11,657k or 63% over four years
findings.quote: The Authority is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Appendices 2026/27
findings.headline: Financing costs as percentage of revenue forecast to rise 45% from 12.09% to 17.58% between 2026/27 and 2030/31
findings.detail: The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream is forecast to increase from 12.09% in 2026/27 to 17.58% in 2030/31. This reflects capital programmes financed primarily through borrowing. By 2030/31, nearly one-fifth of net revenue will be consumed by debt servicing costs, leaving reduced capacity for service delivery and contingencies.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs constrain revenue available for services and limit flexibility to respond to unexpected pressures. Ratio approaching 20% of revenue is material. Lenders assess revenue sustainability; high debt service ratios indicate reduced financial flexibility and increased risk if service demands rise or revenues decline.
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream – General Fund 9.37% 9.75% 12.09% 13.08% 15.64% 17.56% 17.58%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Appendices 2026/27
findings.headline: £1m Lothbury Property Trust investment fund was wound up in May 2024 following value decline, with recovery now being pursued through UBS Triton investment
findings.detail: Council invested £1m in Lothbury Property Trust in December 2019. The fund experienced ongoing value reduction. Fund managers issued termination notice on 31 March 2024, extended to 31 May 2024 after an extraordinary general meeting. A merger option did not proceed. Fund was wound up 30 May 2024. Section 151 Officer determined that transferring proceeds to UBS Triton represented the best opportunity to recover the investment loss.
findings.matters: Represents a material investment loss on £1m and indicates investment governance issues. Lenders assess councils' investment management capability and risk controls. Recovery strategy shows acknowledged loss but does not recover the full amount originally invested.
findings.figures: £1m investment December 2019; fund wound up 30 May 2024
findings.quote: The Council invested £1m in the Lothbury Property Trust in December 2019, following an ongoing reduction in the fund value, fund managers gave notice to terminate the fund on 31st March 2024... the fund was wound up on the 30th May. The Executive Director (Section 151)... determined under delegated authority that the transfer of funds from Lothbury to UBS Triton remained the Council's best opportunity to recover its investment loss

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Analysis of Reserves
findings.headline: Contractual Losses Support Reserve drawn down by £127.5k over two years at £63.75k annually
findings.detail: The Contractual Losses Support Reserve declines from £255k to £127.5k over 2025/26 and 2026/27 at a consistent rate of approximately £63.75k per year, indicating planned funding of specific identified contractual liabilities.
findings.matters: Systematic drawdown of contractual loss reserves confirms the council has identified specific liabilities that require funding over a multi-year period and is actively managing them
findings.figures: £255,000 (March 2025) reducing to £127,500 (March 2027)
findings.quote: Contractual Losses Support Reserve 9999/VBU (255,000) 63,750 (191,250) 63,750 (127,500)

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Analysis of Reserves
findings.headline: General Fund Balance declining by £295k over two years despite planned reserve use
findings.detail: The operational General Fund Balance reduces from £7.25m (March 2025) to £6.95m (March 2027), with movements of £241k and £54k in each year respectively. The reserve is declining despite these positive movements, indicating active use to fund operations.
findings.matters: Declining general reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and ability to absorb unexpected service pressures or income shortfalls without additional borrowing

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Analysis of Reserves
findings.headline: Ongoing Projects Reserve of £3.13m completely depleted during 2025/26
findings.detail: The Ongoing Projects Reserve, standing at £3.13m at March 2025, is entirely withdrawn over 2025/26 and leaves no balance for 2026/27. This represents a complete drawdown of a substantial capital or project fund.
findings.matters: Depletion of a major reserve signals either completion of planned capital commitments or reallocation of funds, with implications for future spending plans and strategic flexibility
findings.figures: £3,130,441 fully withdrawn
findings.quote: Ongoing Projects Reserve 9999/VBM (3,130,441) 3,130,441 0 0

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Analysis of Reserves
findings.headline: NNDR Income Reserve increased 179% to £3.99m, indicating significant business rates income volatility concerns
findings.detail: The council has increased its business rates income buffer from £1.43m to £3.99m during 2025/26, an addition of £2.56m. The reserve then reduces slightly to £3.48m by March 2027. This substantial buildup signals the council expects material volatility in business rates income.
findings.matters: Business rates are a volatile income source post-COVID, and accumulating nearly £4m in reserves indicates the council perceives significant revenue risk that could affect service sustainability and debt servicing capacity
findings.figures: £1,432,502 (March 2025) increasing to £3,988,189 (March 2026)

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: 5 Year Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2030/31 - Report
findings.headline: UK Shared Prosperity Fund grant funding ending after 2025/26
findings.detail: Council received £691,969 UKSPF in 2025/26 with £127,000 designated for capital expenditure. This external funding scheme is not expected to continue for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Loss of grant funding creates a financing gap; demonstrates council dependence on time-limited government grants that will not be available going forward
findings.figures: £691,969 total UKSPF allocation; £127,000 capital element in 2025/26
findings.quote: The UKSPF scheme is not expected to continue for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: 5 Year Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2030/31 - Report
findings.headline: Council acknowledges capital programme schemes may be deferred or stopped if revenue costs become unaffordable
findings.detail: The document explicitly identifies that if revenue implications become prohibitive or available funding changes, schemes may be recommended for deferral or cessation. Officers will monitor progress and costs closely.
findings.matters: Capital programme is not a fixed commitment; council's own risk assessment shows affordability concern; programme could be reduced if budget pressures increase
findings.figures: £81,922 revenue costs in 2026/27; £2,131m over five years
findings.quote: Officers will closely monitor the progress of expenditure against the Capital Programme and, if the revenue implications become prohibitive, because of increasing costs or changes to available funding, schemes may be recommended for deferral.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: 5 Year Capital Programme 2026/27 to 2030/31 - Report
findings.headline: Council proposing £14.18m of borrowing over five years to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The five-year capital programme totals £19.57m, with £2.627m borrowing needed in 2026/27 alone. The council can fund only £0.79m from its own resources and £4.59m from grants, leaving £14.18m to be borrowed. This is a material increase to council debt.
findings.matters: Material borrowing requirement directly affects council's debt position and creditworthiness, influencing lender assessment and future borrowing capacity
findings.figures: £14.18m borrowing 2026/27-2030/31; £19.57m total five-year programme; £2.627m borrowing in 2026/27
findings.quote: Across the life of the 5 Year Capital Programme, it is forecast that just under £0.79m of capital expenditure can be met from the Council's own resources (e.g., capital receipts and reserves), and another £4.59m from capital grants and contributions. This leaves a projected borrowing requirement of £14.18m between 2026/27 and 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review determined that Blaby has fared poorly, with impact masked by Business Rate income treatment in settlement
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review has not treated Blaby favorably. The negative impact of the review on Blaby's allocation has been partially obscured by the way business rate income has been handled within the three-year settlement. This masking effect creates risk that the true impact of the review will become apparent in future settlement periods.
findings.matters: A council that has 'fared poorly' in a major funding review faces structural disadvantage in future settlements; this may represent a permanent downward shift in available funding.
findings.figures: Blaby fared poorly from Fair Funding Review; impact partially masked by business rate treatment
findings.quote: Whilst Blaby hasn't faired well from the review the manner in which Business Rate Income has been treated within the Settlement has somewhat masked the detrimental impact.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: County Council funding cuts creating difficult-to-quantify increased demand for Blaby services
findings.detail: The document notes that Leicestershire County Council has publicly announced significant funding cuts over coming years. Whilst the district council can plan for obvious impacts, some effects are subtle and harder to quantify. The resulting increased demand for services is identified as a considerable risk to which 'financial values will be put as and when we are in a position to do so'—indicating current uncertainty about the scale of the impact.
findings.matters: County council retrenchment is already known to be happening; the council cannot yet quantify its financial impact, creating a hidden budget risk.
findings.figures: Funding cuts from county council; financial impact to be quantified
findings.quote: The County Council has openly illustrated the level of funding cuts that they will be required to make over the coming years. Whilst we can plan to mitigate any obvious impacts of this, some are more subtle and the increased demand that results from this is difficult to quantify financially.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Food waste implementation required by April 2026 with modelled costs that may be exceeded once service goes live
findings.detail: The council is required to implement food waste collection by April 2026. Funding has been provided in the settlement but is not specifically identified. Officers have modelled costs for the service, but there is explicit risk that actual costs could exceed budgeted amounts once demand from residents is understood.
findings.matters: A statutory service starting mid-year with uncertain demand creates cost risk; if budgets are exceeded, the council must fund the overspend immediately.
findings.figures: Service implementation April 2026; costs modelled but subject to demand uncertainty
findings.quote: Funding has been provided within the Settlement; however, it is not specifically identified. Officers have modelled the costs of providing this service, however until the service 'goes live' and demand levels from residents are understood, there is a risk costs could exceed those budgeted.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Homelessness costs rising with only partial mitigation through property investment funded by external schemes
findings.detail: The council reports a considerable increase in homelessness costs and acknowledges potential for further increases. Whilst additional budget allocation has been made and the council is investing in temporary accommodation properties using Local Authority Housing Fund and council investment, the underlying demand trend is uncertain.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness demand is placing pressure on budgets; if the trend accelerates, it could create an unplanned overspend in a key statutory service.
findings.figures: Considerable increase in homelessness costs; additional expenditure budgeted
findings.quote: We have seen a considerable increase in homelessness costs and whilst allowance has been made in the budget for additional expenditure there is the potential for costs to continue to increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Local Government Reform transition costs at risk of exceeding budgeted amounts due to unresolved cost-sharing arrangements
findings.detail: £700k is budgeted in 2026/27 for LGR preparation with a further £700k to be released from reserves in 2027/28. However, there is no agreement between Leicestershire authorities on how transition costs will be shared, creating explicit risk that Blaby's final share will exceed these provisional sums.
findings.matters: LGR is a structural change with uncertain financial implications; unexpected cost overruns could force the council to draw down reserves more heavily than planned.
findings.figures: £700k budgeted 2026/27; £700k from reserves 2027/28 (provisional)
findings.quote: These are provisional sums and currently there is no agreement between authorities in Leicestershire as to how transition costs might be shared to form the new unitary authorities. As such, there is a risk that Blaby's share of transition costs is greater than the amounts allowed for.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £1.6m forecast to decline by 20-30% over MTFS period
findings.detail: £1.6m of EPR funding from Defra based on recycling tonnages is included in 2026/27 but at risk of substantial reduction. The council has modelled 20% reduction from 2027/28 and 10% reduction in following years, and notes MHCLG has raised concerns about the longevity of this funding stream. Future reductions could come from consumer deposit schemes reducing collected tonnages.
findings.matters: This represents a material and declining income source with uncertain future levels; the council may be forced to downscale operations to match funding.
findings.figures: £1.6m EPR funding 2026/27; 20% reduction modelled from 2027/28; 10% reduction in following years
findings.quote: Funding of £1.6m has been included in 2026/27 budget figures from Defra relating to the Extended Producer Responsibility for Packaging (EPR)... The MTFS has modelled for a reduction of 20% in EPR from 2027/28 and a 10% reduction in the years following.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Business Rates funding uncertain from 2029/30 onwards despite three-year settlement protection
findings.detail: The three-year settlement protects 95% of historical business rate income through 2028/29, but there is substantial uncertainty about whether this protection continues beyond 2029/30. Transitional funding rises to £3.03m by 2028/29, indicating significant damping protection is masking underlying funding reductions.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core revenue source; if protection is withdrawn as planned, the council faces an immediate cliff-edge funding reduction in 2029/30.
findings.figures: 95% protection through settlement; transitional funding rises to £3.03m in 2028/29
findings.quote: Whilst the 3-year Settlement has protected 95% of the income historically generated through growth and the Business Rate Pool, it is unknown as to what extent this will be retained from 2029/30 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C – Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) including Plan to Close Future financial Gaps
findings.headline: Budget gap forecast to reach £2.6m in 2028/29, potentially £6.7m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The MTFS projects widening budget gaps over the forecast period. The council identifies £2.6m gap in 2028/29, rising to potentially £6.7m in 2030/31 if all transitional funding is lost. This represents a substantial and growing funding shortfall with high uncertainty beyond 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible plan to close growing budget gaps and whether transformation initiatives are likely to succeed.
findings.figures: £2.6m budget gap 2028/29; potential £6.7m gap 2030/31
findings.quote: The MTFS suggests that there will be a budget gap of £2.6m in 2028/29 which could rise to £6.7m in 2030/31 of all transitional funding is lost.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: S151 Officer formally questions whether reserves are adequate given LGR costs and homelessness demand
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (Executive Director) explicitly states in her formal Section 25 opinion: 'there is a question as to whether the reserves are sufficient to underpin future financial pressures' caused by LGR uncertainty and ongoing demand-led spending (particularly homelessness).
findings.matters: The council's chief finance officer has flagged reserve adequacy concerns in her statutory opinion—the strongest governance warning available; this signals financial stress ahead
findings.figures: Not applicable; qualitative governance concern
findings.quote: Given the uncertainty as to how the costs of implementation of LGR are to be funded and the continuing costs of demand-led services, such as homeless, there is a question as to whether the reserves are sufficient to underpin future financial pressures.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: MTFS forecasts funding deficits of £3.7m–£6.7m by 2030/31 depending on transitional grant continuation
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy models a significant structural deficit opening within four years. If transitional funding (currently £3.04m in 2028/29) ceases entirely, the 2030/31 gap reaches £6.7m.
findings.matters: Looming structural deficit will require major intervention: service cuts, major council tax rises, or merger into unitary authority cannot proceed without fiscal restructuring
findings.figures: £3.7m gap (if transitional funding continues); £6.7m gap (if transitional funding ceases) in 2030/31
findings.quote: The transitional funding in 2028/29 is £3.04m, should transitional funding continue to be included the financial gap in year 2030/31 increases to £3.7m, if transitional funding were to cease this gap would increase to £6.7m.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Council drawing £1.06m from reserves in 2026/27 to balance current budget
findings.detail: The council proposes withdrawing £1.004m from earmarked reserves (including £505.7k from NNDR Income Reserve) and £54k from General Fund Balance to support the 2026/27 budget. This includes draws to fund leisure contract income shortfalls and homelessness services.
findings.matters: Reserve draw-down to fund recurring operations signals inability to fund services from current revenues; reduces financial flexibility for future shocks or LGR costs
findings.figures: £1,004,643 from earmarked reserves; £53,959 from General Fund Balance
findings.quote: In 2026/27 it is proposed that the Council makes a contribution of £1,004,643 from earmarked reserves to support the budget

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Defra Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £1.6m flagged by MHCLG as having uncertain longevity
findings.detail: The council includes £1.6m in 2026/27 from Defra EPR funding (up from £1.5m in 2025/26). However, MHCLG has formally raised concerns about whether this funding will continue beyond the current arrangement.
findings.matters: Loss of this funding would leave a £1.6m hole requiring service cuts or reserve draw; MHCLG's explicit concern suggests possible discontinuation
findings.quote: Comments made by MHCLG have raised concerns as to the longevity of this funding stream.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Business Rates baseline reset permanently reduces council's retained income by 37% from £5.6m to £3.5m
findings.detail: The government baseline reset redistributes retained rates income by relative need. Blaby's retained business rates income drops materially. The council will no longer benefit from business rates growth in its district due to the reset.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural loss of revenue-raising capacity; the council must either cut services or raise council tax to replace it
findings.figures: £5.6m (2025/26) reducing to £3.5m (2026/27 before £505.7k reserve draw)
findings.quote: the baseline reset has considerably reduced the amount of Business Rate income retained by Blaby District Council reducing the income to £3.5m before releasing £506k from the NNDR Income Reserve. This is a reduction from 2025/26 levels of £5.6m.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: General Fund Budget Proposals 2026/27 - Report
findings.headline: Adjustment Support Grant of £1.382m has no commitment beyond 2026/27, creating a funding cliff
findings.detail: The council received a one-off adjustment support grant to compensate for changes in the business rates settlement. The grant is explicitly for 2026/27 only, with no guarantee of continuation. The S151 Officer notes this has increased MTFS gaps for years after 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council is balancing its 2026/27 budget with ~£1.4m of one-off funding; losing this in 2027/28 will require immediate service cuts or reserves draw
findings.figures: £1.382m in 2026/27; no commitment beyond this year
findings.quote: There is no commitment that this grant will continue beyond 2026/27 and the Final Settlement shows this grant being for one year only, as a result the gaps in the MTFS for years after 2026/27 have increased.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Fleet vehicle replacement programme of £7.7m locks in multi-year revenue costs via borrowing and MRP at critical time
findings.detail: Essential fleet replacement totals £7.7m over five years, predominantly in years 2–5. This creates fixed revenue commitments through loan interest and Minimum Revenue Provision that will burden a budget already projected to have a £6.7m deficit.
findings.matters: Large, inflexible capital commitments lock in future revenue costs precisely when the council's budget position is deteriorating
findings.figures: Fleet Vehicle Replacement Programme: £7,740,000 over five years; peak year spend: £2,955,000 in 2030/31

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council will transition from internal borrowing to external PWLB debt when rates fall to 5%, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council is currently using internal cash reserves to fund capital spending (cheaper than external borrowing). However, it states this 'cannot be sustained' and will shift to external PWLB borrowing once rates fall to approximately 5%. This creates timing uncertainty about when £14.2m of new external debt will be drawn, plus rate refinancing risk.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of when external debt will be drawn and at what rates, as this determines future debt serviceability against an already-deficit budget
findings.figures: £14.2m total borrowing planned over five years; external borrowing threshold: approximately 5% PWLB rates
findings.quote: This position cannot be sustained in the longer term and, as the Council's reserves and balances diminish over the life of the current MTFS, it will be necessary to drawdown new borrowing

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Available reserves declining 60% to £196k by 2030, eliminating financial flexibility while borrowing rises
findings.detail: Unallocated reserves fall from £478k to £196k over the planning period—a loss of £282k of financial buffer. This occurs simultaneously with planned borrowing of £14.2m. The council will have minimal reserves to manage emergencies or unexpected costs while carrying significantly increased debt.
findings.matters: Declining reserves combined with rising debt worsens the council's financial resilience and its ability to weather shocks or service disruptions
findings.figures: Unallocated reserves: £478k (31/03/26) falling to £196k (31/03/30); total unallocated resources: £1,138k falling to £683k

findings.paper_title: Appendix B – Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Projected budget deficit of £6.7m by 2030/31 signals structural financial unsustainability
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy projects a significant budget deficit by the end of the five-year planning period. This deficit indicates the council will be unable to balance its budget through normal service revenues and will face difficult choices about service reductions, tax increases, or further borrowing.
findings.matters: A council projecting a structural deficit presents elevated credit risk to lenders and indicates the finance director faces severe financial stress within the planning period
findings.figures: £6.7m budget deficit by 2030/31
findings.quote: The MTFS predicts a budget deficit of £6.7m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: IT control weaknesses identified: third-party risk assessment process not implemented and MFA deployment incomplete
findings.detail: Auditors identified that the council does not have a process to assess cyber risk in suppliers and third parties either at procurement or during contracts. Additionally, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication has not been implemented across all systems. These issues were carried forward from prior observations.
findings.matters: Weak IT controls and incomplete security implementation increase risk of data breach or financial system compromise, which could affect financial data integrity.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; findings categorized as Amber (developing) priority
findings.quote: The Council does not proactively perform sufficient and appropriate risk assessment of third parties to identify cyber threats and vulnerabilities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Audit working papers were of mixed quality and required multiple clarifications from management
findings.detail: The finance team submitted working papers that were often incomplete or poorly documented, requiring the audit team to repeatedly request clarifications and additional support. This delayed progress and is attributed to the council having had no full audit since 2019/20. Examples include receiving spreadsheets without proper supporting documentation and needing to speak to various staff members to piece together single areas.
findings.matters: Mixed-quality working papers indicate internal control weaknesses in financial record-keeping and documentation; suggests the council may not have adequate controls over its financial processes.
findings.figures: No full audit since 2019/20 (gap of 5+ years)
findings.quote: Working papers received were of mixed quality. We experienced some occasions of needing to go back to management to clarify what we needed and to ensure that the quality of the working papers was appropriate. Given the Council has not experienced a full audit since 2019/20, this was expected.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Pension liability of £7.3m has no audit assurance and cannot be verified
findings.detail: The council's defined benefit pension liability stands at £7.3m, but the auditors have no assurance over opening balances or year-on-year movements because prior years were disclaimed. They deferred audit work on this until 2025/26 when a new triennial valuation is due. Without prior assurance, they cannot conclude on the material accuracy of the 2024/25 valuation.
findings.matters: A large contingent liability with no audit verification creates undefined risk to the council's financial position and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £7,308,000 defined pension fund liability; £7,459,396 total other long-term liabilities
findings.quote: This means we have no assurance on the movements in year and cannot gain sufficient audit evidence on the material accuracy of the valuation of the pension fund liability as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Blaby District Council Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Auditors disclaim their opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements due to prior year assurance gaps
findings.detail: The auditors cannot form an unmodified opinion on the 2024/25 accounts. Despite completing most work, they lack sufficient assurance on opening balances and transactions from four prior years (2020/21 through 2023/24) that also had disclaimed opinions. The statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026 prevented completion of all planned procedures.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means no independent verification of the council's financial position; lenders have no third-party assurance of the accuracy of reported reserves, assets or liabilities.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, now including 2024/25
findings.quote: Due to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous four years have been disclaimed, it has not been possible for us to undertake sufficient work to regain full assurance and support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will divert management capacity from delivering planned savings until council merges in April 2028.
findings.detail: Blaby is one of seven Leicestershire councils developing proposals to merge into three unitary authorities, with transition April 2028. This reorganisation requires significant management time and external skills. The auditor specifically identifies that this may divert attention from delivering planned savings, making achievement of previously planned savings less likely.
findings.matters: The council's ability to bridge its £12.692m funding gap depends on delivering transformational savings. If management is diverted to reorganisation for three years, these savings may not be realised, worsening the structural funding position at a critical time.
findings.figures: Reorganisation runs 2025-2028; council ceases to exist April 2028
findings.quote: Plans and arrangements for reorganisation will take up increasing capacity of senior officers and this may divert attention from the realisation of savings plans or make the achievement of previously planned savings less likely.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Council's financial plan depends on £3.3 million of unconfirmed government damping that may not materialise.
findings.detail: To bridge the funding gap from the Fair Funding Review, the MTFS assumes the government will introduce a damping mechanism to smooth funding reductions over three years, providing £3.3m from 2026/27. The auditor notes this is not a confirmed or guaranteed amount. If damping is lower or does not occur, residual funding gaps would increase substantially.
findings.matters: The council's financial recovery plan relies on £3.3m of hoped-for government funding that is explicitly unconfirmed. If this does not materialise, the structural funding gap widens, forcing more severe service reductions or faster reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £3.3m damping assumption in MTFS from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: This is not a confirmed or guaranteed amount and would be expected to be in the form of additional funding.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Funding gaps totalling £12.692 million over five years will deplete reserves below the council's own policy minimum.
findings.detail: Budget gaps range from £1.1m in 2026/27 to £4.9m in 2029/30. After planned transformational savings and efficiency initiatives, residual gaps remain: £534k (2026/27), £336k (2027/28), £2.165m (2028/29), £2.737m (2029/30). The council has sufficient reserves to cover these gaps but only by falling below its policy range of 10-45% of net budget requirement.
findings.matters: Reserves provide the buffer to absorb unexpected shocks. Once depleted below policy minimum, the council will have no resilience against further funding cuts, inflation, or demand pressures.
findings.figures: Total funding gaps £12.692m over five years; residual funding gaps 2026/27-2029/30 total £5.772m after identified savings
findings.quote: This would still leave the general fund in a positive position, albeit, the reserves balance would fall below the Council's minimum requirements during this period.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Business Rates Baseline Reset in 2026/27 will cut council income by £3.924 million in a single year.
findings.detail: The council has benefited from significant business rates growth since 2013. A reset of the baseline in 2026/27 will eliminate this benefit. The Medium Term Financial Strategy shows business rates income collapsing from £5.511m in 2025/26 to £1.587m in 2026/27. The council plans to draw £860k annually from its NNDR income reserve but this leaves approximately £3m of the income loss unmitigated.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent structural loss of income that cannot be recovered. The council will need to either reduce services or draw down reserves to cover this gap, reducing its financial resilience.
findings.figures: Business rates income drops from £5.511m to £1.587m (£3.924m reduction); council budgets to draw £860k annually from NNDR reserve 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: The MTFS currently includes income from Business Rates of £5.511m in 2025/26 to £1.587m in 2026/27, which is a significant reduction.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report Appendix A
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of auditor opinion disclaimer means accounts cannot be verified.
findings.detail: Due to cumulative effect of four prior years of disclaimed opinions, the auditor has been unable to obtain full assurance on opening and closing balances in key areas by the statutory deadline of 27 February 2026. The auditor expects to disclaim the opinion for 2024/25 as well, meaning the financial position cannot be formally verified.
findings.matters: A lender cannot properly assess the council's actual financial position without audited accounts. Four years of unaudited statements represents a material governance failure and means the council's reported reserves and financial position cannot be relied upon.
findings.figures: Fourth consecutive year of auditor opinion disclaimer
findings.quote: We therefore expect to disclaim our audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - 6 Month Progress Report on Actions Arising from Annual Governance Assurance Review November 2025
findings.headline: Risk management framework has gaps in lower-level risk recording and focus
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that work remains to ensure lower-level risks receive appropriate attention and are properly recorded in the I-Plan system. This suggests the internal control environment does not yet fully cover all risks across the organisation.
findings.matters: Weak risk management can allow financial or operational problems to surface unexpectedly; a lender would want confidence that the council's control environment is robust.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: more work is needed to ensure the lower-level risks have the right level of focus and recording.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - 6 Month Progress Report on Actions Arising from Annual Governance Assurance Review November 2025
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is forcing shorter-term partnership agreements
findings.detail: The council has shortened partnership terms for the Lightbulb Service and Housing Enablement Team (HET) due to the potential impact of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). This means the council is planning for major structural change and faces uncertainty about future service delivery and financial arrangements from April 2026.
findings.matters: LGR would fundamentally restructure the council and affect its financial stability, borrowing capacity, and service continuity; a lender needs to understand the scale of this uncertainty and whether the council has a funding plan for the transition.
findings.figures: April 2026
findings.quote: Agreements have now been made for shorter a time period given the potential impact of LGR.
